#SexIndustryArticles

Move fast and break women - on Meta's smart glasses and the gendered costs of reckless, unregulated innovation

https://t.co/HSG92gNKRG

"One morning, on my way to high school, a teenage boy slid into the bus seat beside me. He told me he lived nearby and that we went to the same school. Then, just as casually as if he were commenting on the weather, he added that he liked taking pictures of me when I was running.

When I relayed the story to my female friends, nauseous at the idea of a stranger creeping on me like this, they said similar things had happened to them, too. This was the early 2010s; almost every phone already had a built-in camera. Boys then used them to try to snap pictures of girls walking upstairs in skirts. Or in bathrooms. Or changing before PE. And sometimes, those photos were also shared around, including the ones girls had sent in confidence to just one boy.

I quickly internalised the message that these things ‘just happen,’ that this is an unpleasant but inevitable feature of girlhood — and, later, womanhood — not least because there were rarely any consequences for boys who did them. What can you do? Boys will be boys.

Today, we treat newer forms of technology-facilitated harassment and abuse in much the same way. Each time a new tool appears, men and boys find ways to weaponise it against us, while the companies that launch it and the public mostly give a collective shrug. These things just happen.

The latest addition to that digital abuse toolkit? Meta’s smart glasses.

Smart glasses are essentially smartphones for your face. They can send messages, answer questions, and record photos and videos, all hands-free. Meta’s latest AI-powered version, dubbed Meta Glasses, is also virtually indistinguishable from an ordinary pair of designer frames. The company even enlisted Kylie Jenner and a slew of other influencers to promote the product.

So how can you know if someone wearing these Cybertrucks of eyewear is recording you? In theory, the glasses turn on a small LED light whenever recording begins. In practice, the internet is full of step-by-step tutorials on how to cover the light or deactivate it altogether.

Meta’s ‘hands-free companion’ might market itself as a tool helping people live in the moment and ‘capture life,’ but it has also made it easier than ever to capture the lives of people who never agreed to it — and who likely won’t even realise it’s happening. And, unsurprisingly, most of those being filmed non-consensually are women.

A recent CNN investigation found that some men wearing Meta’s smart glasses have been secretly recording themselves approaching women in public and attempting to pick them up. The footage is then uploaded to their social media accounts without the women’s consent or knowledge, racking up millions of views and thousands of comments — many of them sexually explicit and abusive — all while generating revenue for the ‘creators’ behind it. None of the women CNN spoke with reported seeing the glasses’ recording light during these encounters. And even those who contacted the men to ask for the videos to be removed had little success. As other reports have also shown, experiences like this usually leave women humiliated, distraught, and feeling stripped of their right to move freely through public spaces. One woman told the BBC:

I had no idea it was happening to me, I didn’t consent to that being posted, I didn’t consent to being secretly filmed. It really freaked me out — it made me feel afraid to go out in public.

Meta’s response was as predictable as the harassment itself. In statements to media outlets covering the story, the company said it was aware of a ‘small number of users’ choosing to ‘misuse’ its products, while stressing that it would ‘continually review opportunities to enhance our AI glasses informed by customer feedback.’

This reminds me of what happened with another of Meta’s recent ventures: the Metaverse and its virtual reality platform Horizon Worlds, built for the modest sum of ‘just’ $80 billion. Even during its early development, Horizon users reported being harassed and abused online. And when one beta tester said they were ‘groped,’ describing the experience as more ‘intense’ than online sexual harassment, Meta’s then-VP of Horizon, Vivek Sharma, merely responded that the incident was ‘unfortunate.’

As Laura Bates writes in her brilliant new book, The New Age of Sexism:

For Meta, women’s online experiences of harassment and abuse are all helpful fodder for improving their product and making more money out of it. The ‘make it now and fix any safety issues later’ approach has never been more clearly on display.

And, as could also be predicted, that beta tester was just the first of many, mostly female, victims.1 The safety features Meta later pointed to weren’t always easy to find, nor did they consistently work. Horizon Worlds then quickly became a cesspool of sexually explicit content, racism, grooming, sexual harassment, and abuse — including against children.

This is all a familiar Big Tech script: Move fast. Break things (though mostly women and girls). Worry about the harm done later on. Or don’t even bother. Rinse and repeat."

In 6 months of vibe coding I spent $20,000.
Revenue so far: $125.
Not exactly a TechCrunch headline.

After the war with Iran hit, my businesses in Dubai (a beach club and a cafe) started losing money.

That was the moment I realized I needed to diversify and I went deep into AI.

Claude. Codex. Agents. Tokens. Domains. Vercel. Supabase. Replicate. Cloudflare. Resend.
For 6 months, I vibe coded every single day.

Here’s what I launched:

1/ https://t.co/EAT7hEt39L: An AI chat app that learns your website and replies to customers.

2/ https://t.co/k9EFSGBkHs: A QR menu for restaurants with beautiful designs, AI photo generation, and tools to help cafes/restaurants improve service and increase sales.

3/ https://t.co/TgJr61W5jm: Currently in beta. An app for fashion photographers and brands to create graphic content for websites, ads, and social media.

4/ https://t.co/eSeEqJC3MZ: A site that turns simple phone pictures into professional family portraits.

5/ https://t.co/D7Qr6iJ6wt: A 2048 game website because I was too frustrated with the original one.

I also built and killed more than 20 projects that never launched.

Total spent: around $20k (not bad considering I have launched five businesses)

Subscriptions. Tokens. Domains. Freelance devs to fix the vibe-coded mess.
Total revenue: $125.

A few lessons from the trenches:

1. Architecture is everything.
AI can help you move fast, but if the foundation is bad, every new feature becomes painful. Spend time understanding the architecture of your project before shipping too many features on top of it.

2. Building products is addicting. I keep delaying the part where I have to sell what I built.

3. Good products take many iterations.
I usually build an app, use it, break it, change it, rebuild parts of it, and only ship after 20–25 iterations. For me, it takes around 2 weeks of full-time work to go from idea to something launchable.

4. Vibe coding does not replace engineering.
I rely on @deifosv to make sure there are no major security issues, bugs, or disasters hiding under the surface.

5. Product is not “easy now.”
People say marketing is hard and product is easy because of AI. I disagree. Building a useful product with good UI still takes a lot of prompting, testing, taste, and patience.

6. Marketing is even harder.
I tried posting daily on TikTok, Instagram, and other platforms. It is brutal if you already have another business/job. I’m now considering hiring a growth marketer or content creator.

7. AI tools are incredible, but they don’t remove the grind.
They just let you grind faster.

8. My current stack favorites:
Replicate, Cloudflare, Vercel, Supabase, Resend.

Reward-guided diffusion: reinforcement learning steers generative models toward novel, stable crystals

Anyone who trains generative models knows the tension. A diffusion model fit by maximum likelihood learns to reproduce its training distribution, so it samples what looks familiar. In materials discovery, though, the interesting compounds sit in the low-probability tails, the underexplored regions where genuinely new structures live. Sampling more of the same is exactly what you do not want.

Hyunsoo Park and Aron Walsh reframe this as a post-training problem. Instead of nudging outputs with heuristics like classifier-free guidance, they fine-tune the model with reinforcement learning, optimizing explicit rewards rather than data likelihood. The move that makes it tractable: they run diffusion in a compressed VAE latent space, which turns the awkward mix of discrete atom types and continuous coordinates into a homogeneous action space where policy gradients behave.

The engine is GRPO, the same group-relative policy optimization behind recent reasoning LLMs, here driving a denoising diffusion policy. The reward is multi-objective and, crucially, verifiable: a creativity term for uniqueness and novelty, a stability term using a machine-learning force field as a fast proxy for DFT energy above the convex hull, and a diversity term that blocks mode collapse.

The payoff is a clean shift of the Pareto frontier. On the Alex-MP-20 benchmark, their metastable-unique-novel score jumps from 15.9% to 61.3%, novelty climbs from 62.3% to 97.5%, and metastability still rises from 51.2% to 72.1%. Novelty and stability usually trade off, and here RL buys both at once. The same framework handles inverse design too: targeting a 3 eV bandgap, RL keeps chemical validity intact while classifier-free guidance collapses to near-zero.

For discovery pipelines in batteries, catalysis, or semiconductors, the practical takeaway is that a verifiable reward plus policy optimization can redirect a generative model toward candidates worth synthesizing, not merely plausible ones. Swap the reward and the same machinery targets ionic conductivity, formation energy, or a specific gap, giving a modular path from "generates something reasonable" to "generates what the program actually needs."

Paper: Park et al., Nature Machine Intelligence (2026), CC BY 4.0 | https://t.co/4cwgBOxl0F
